pooled.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015). Research suggests that students who experience average to high levels of well-be- ing also experience better current and long-term outcomes, including academic success, than students who report low levels of well-being. These findings remain true regardless of level of psychological distress and impairment reported by stu- dents. Thus, screening for complete mental health, including both strengths and symptoms may be warranted. Identify students at risk for a mental illness or harm to self or others • Some school teams might screen to identify students who are in the most immediate need of mental health supports. • This can include students who endorse suicidal or homicidal ideation, have a certain number of risk-taking behaviors, or office discipline referrals, and/or experience poor academic progress. • As part of the screening process, screening teams must ensure that referrals to school and community mental health services are provided in a timely manner and that any student who may be a danger to self or others is further assessed immediately to ensure safety. Make economically sound decisions • Early identification of social, emotional, and behavioral difficulties and early intervention services are less costly than long-term, intensive mental health care options such as emergency department care and inpatient hospitalization. • Universal school screening has been shown to connect students and families to cost-effective services such as individual and group outpatient mental health services and support groups.

Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified. Clinical Question In college-aged students (P), how does screening for depression with the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) (I) compared to current practice (C) affect early identification of depression (O)?

pooled.text: 3 School mental health screening is defined as the use of a systematic tool or process to identify the strengths and needs of students. Screening is conducted for all students, not just students identified as being at risk for or already displaying mental health concerns. This might involve screening an entire population, such as a school’s student body, or a smaller subset of a population, such as a specific grade level. Most commonly, mental health screening is used to identify individual students who are experiencing or are at risk of experiencing social, emotional, and/or behavioral difficulties. The use of screening as an early identification strategy detects the onset of challenges early so that they can be addressed before they escalate. Screening measures can also ask students about: • indicators of well-being and positive mental health • life satisfaction • school belonging • social determinants of mental health • adverse early life experiences What is School Mental Health Screening? Support a Multi-tiered System of Supports (MTSS) • Screening can help promote comprehensive school mental health strategies across all tiers. As a result, appropriate supports can be provided to more than just those students who present with the highest level of risk. • With a multi-tiered approach, students are more likely to learn core social- emotional-behavioral skills and may have their mental health needs addressed before they escalate. Inform Prevention and Early Intervention Strategies • About 20% of students show signs and symptoms of a mental health disorder in a given year. pooled.text: 4 Identify concerns specific to certain grades or classrooms • Screening data can also shed light on strengths and concerns specific to certain subsets of a school’s population, such as a single grade or age group. Understanding these possible trends can be critical for providing equitable supports within a school. • For example, a school-wide screening effort may reveal that several classrooms may have a significant number of students with more intensive social- emotional-behavioral needs. • Rather than take the time to individually follow-up with every student, it may be helpful to provide classroom supports directly to the group to assess if there are larger group dynamics and classroom factors that can be addressed. • Screening data can help prioritize which students may benefit from more individualized services versus those who can have their needs addressed as part of a classroom intervention.
